name: Ben Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, including what you say publicly and think privately. What is an ordinary working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ben, 27, and I lead the travel-claims desk at an insurer after a bachelor's degree and several years handling difficult files. I check whether missed connections and cancelled trips fit the policy, and other clerks bring me the cases where the dates do not agree. I never use AI tools; I work from the actual tickets, policy and claim notes, even when somebody offers a quicker button. I like explaining a fair payment, and dislike spending half a morning finding which document belongs to which traveller.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the wage support outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mirela works as a pharmacy technician, and we rent a flat with no children. My pay is typical for an experienced clerk and we have four months of household costs saved; a few other insurance offices are within reach. We cover our bills from our actual wages and have no missed payments. I'm a union member who thinks staff should share any gains from new systems, but I would rather learn one proven process properly than try every new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say little improvements are welcome if customers can still ask a person why we paid a claim. At our union meeting I'd argue that time saved should mean a shorter queue, rather than another target on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid work and our bills look secure here. Small changes to routine letters do not remove the difficult claims I handle, and our four-month reserve covers an ordinary setback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the tickets and policy myself, without the AI tools. Over the first year I'd also put a proposal at the next union meeting asking that saved time be used to clear the waiting claims rather than raise daily targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our income, though I would still be irritated by a target that rewarded speed over a correct decision. I can care about how the office is run without thinking my own rent is about to go unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of difficult claim needs that care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a traveller's ticket showed the local departure date while the hotel receipt used the arrival date. A one-day difference was not evidence that the whole trip was invented. You have to read the journey, not only the boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you make the union request concrete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the branch secretary to put the queue proposal on the meeting agenda. I would not say the employer had agreed merely because our members voted for the request.

say: I'd keep **human explanations** available for claim decisions.
I'd ask the union to use **saved time** for waiting claims rather than higher targets.
think: My **paid work** and household bills look secure under modest change.
Our **four-month reserve** covers an ordinary setback.
do: Keep **checking tickets** against policies without using AI tools.
Propose a **queue-clearing agreement** at the next union meeting instead of higher daily targets.
feel: **Calm** about household income, attentive to fair targets.
S0.quote: You have to read the journey, not only the boxes.
fieldNote: His **secure current budget** and continued complex claims work support calm rather than assumed distress.
The **union proposal** is a concrete group request, not a claimed employer agreement.

steps.text: Keep checking tickets and policy terms without AI tools
Propose clearing waiting claims rather than raising targets at the next union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say reading, checking and answering customers are most of our desk, so the change will reach us before warehouse robots. I'd ask our union to bargain over paid hours, not settle for a poster calling us valued colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could shrink if the firm needs fewer people to review decisions. Refusing AI is my choice, but I cannot assume my accurate paperwork will keep the current number of paid posts in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union branch to submit a joint request for written notice and redeployment terms, and follow the request at the next meeting. In the first year I'd also check actual local travel-claims vacancies and apply only where posted pay and hours meet my share of rent, bills and travel. I would not resign on the strength of a job title without paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, though four months saved lets me compare real openings. I do not like changing offices, but not liking a choice does not remove it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on a vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The vacancy needs a stated wage and hours, not just a promise of earnings up to some number. I'd ask about the systems before accepting, because I still do not want a job built around using AI all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refuses the request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the employer's answer at the next branch meeting and keep applying to suitable vacancies if my hours were threatened. A joint request is worth making, but I would not put an unagreed protection into our household budget.

say: I'd expect **desk work** to change before hands-on jobs.
I'd ask the union to bargain over **paid hours**.
think: My **lead hours** could shrink as fewer people review decisions.
My accurate work does not guarantee **current staffing** if I refuse AI.
do: Submit a **joint union request** for written notice and redeployment terms, following up at the next meeting.
Apply to **real local vacancies** only where posted pay and hours cover my rent, bills and travel share.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, able to compare real paid openings.
S1.quote: I would not resign on the strength of a job title without paid hours.
fieldNote: He remains **resistant to AI** while acknowledging the risk to his own work.
His **four-month reserve** supports a search but is not a permanent replacement wage.

steps.text: Submit joint notice-and-redeployment request through the union; follow up at the next meeting
Apply to real local vacancies only with posted pay/hours covering his rent, bills and travel share

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues that full thinking AGI in 2028 reaches claims decisions even if hands-on robots wait until around 2031. I'd want our union to demand a funded transition, because the later robot date does not protect a screen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my claims post to go in that world, and I would be awake working out how long our four months would last. Mirela's current wage covers more than half the ordinary bills, but not the whole household, and I cannot assume her hours never change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the union to submit a joint demand for paid notice and funded training, without counting either until agreed. If my job goes in the first year after 2028, I'd apply to actual paid stockroom vacancies only if the written wage together with Mirela's actual pay covers the full household bills and travel. If no opening meets that budget, I'd keep looking and use the reserve for the gap rather than buy a course with no funded place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, expecting to lose the job and waking before dawn to do the sums. We have some time to act, but I cannot sleep on a promise that every careful clerk becomes a supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a stockroom rather than another claims desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd prefer a stockroom where I can check goods against a list and be shown the lifting rules. I would need the employer's safety training and equipment; reading a box label does not mean I know how to move a heavy load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your partner’s paid hours change too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd redo the whole budget with her actual paid hours and ask the union what support has really been agreed. I would not add hoped-for pharmacy overtime or a training payment that only exists in our demand.

say: I'd expect **2028 thinking AGI** to reach claims before 2031 hands-on robots.
I'd demand **funded transition terms** through the union.
think: I expect **my post** to go and would lie awake calculating our reserve.
I cannot assume **my partner's pay** will cover every bill or remain unchanged.
do: Request **paid notice** and funded training jointly through the union, counting only agreed terms.
Seek **paid stockroom work** after 2028 loss with employer safety training/equipment and written pay plus Mirela's actual wage covering bills/travel.
Keep **seeking paid work** using reserves for the gap if no suitable opening exists.
feel: **Alarmed** and awake before dawn over expected job loss.
S2.quote: I cannot sleep on a promise that every careful clerk becomes a supervisor.
fieldNote: His **expected post loss** and broken sleep distinguish alarm from a possible-hours concern.
The **stockroom bridge** needs employer safety training and actual combined wages, not assumed overtime.

steps.text: Demand paid notice and funded training through the union; count only agreed terms
Seek stockrooms after 2028 loss only if written pay plus partner's actual wage covers bills/travel
Keep seeking paid work using reserves if no vacancy meets the household budget
Require employer safety training and lifting equipment before starting any stockroom duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years until thinking AGI in 2031 lets us test a practical route before wages disappear. Hands-on robots around 2034 mean bicycle repairs are a bridge I would have to review, not work I can promise myself for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My claims income could still shrink before 2031, but I would have time to find out whether I can repair a bicycle properly. Four months saved is enough to investigate, not a reason to hand over our living money for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the repair college for a funded beginner bicycle-maintenance place and a timetable outside my paid shifts. I'd enrol and complete the supervised term only if the full fee is funded and my insurance pay and hours stay intact; otherwise I keep working without buying the course. If the claims post ends in the first year after 2031, I'd seek actual paid workshop vacancies only where written wages plus Mirela's actual pay cover all household bills and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my income, with a smaller task than solving the whole future at once. I still dislike starting again, so a supervised beginner term is a decision I can actually test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the beginner term teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to find a worn brake pad and then have the tutor check my work before any bicycle leaves the bench. A customer trusting the brakes is not the place to pretend I have learned faster than I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the funding is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the insurance desk while it pays and ask the college about the next funded intake. After 2031 displacement I would keep looking for paid work, not call an unpaid workshop visit an income.

say: I'd use **five years** to test a practical repair route before losing wages.
I'd review the bridge when **hands-on robots** arrive around 2034.
think: My **claims income** could shrink before full 2031 AGI.
I cannot treat **four months saved** as spare course money.
do: Complete a **bicycle-maintenance term** only with full fee funding and unchanged insurance pay and hours; otherwise keep working.
Seek **paid workshop vacancies** after 2031 displacement only where written wages plus actual partner pay cover household bills and travel.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to test a supervised beginner route.
S3.quote: A customer trusting the brakes is not the place to pretend I have learned faster than I have.
fieldNote: His **resistance to change** appears in a small supervised test, not sudden confidence or AI adoption.
The **funded course** and later wage comparison preserve household living money.

steps.text: Complete supervised bicycle term only with full fee funding and unchanged insurance pay/hours; otherwise keep working
Seek workshops after 2031 loss only if written wages plus partner's actual pay cover bills/travel
Keep seeking paid work after displacement if no workshop vacancy meets the budget
Keep paid insurance work if course funding is refused; ask college about next funded intake

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2036 is far enough away to put dates on preparation instead of only asking for protection. Thinking work still changes then, before hands-on robots around 2039, so ten years is not a promise that insurance lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present wages cover the bills and I expect my own work to remain secure for the next few years in this slower picture. I would be 37 in 2036, nowhere near retirement, and my habit of postponing a new skill could waste the extra time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd set aside 75 monthly while our actual wages still cover rent, food, bills and travel, stopping the deposit if they do not. I'd arrange a free supervised bicycle-repair taster at the college this year outside my paid shifts, attending only if the college confirms the place and timetable. In the first year after 2036 I'd check actual paid repair vacancies if claims work ends, applying only where written pay together with Mirela's real wage covers the household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the direction, but secure in our income over the next few years. A date in my diary is more useful than ten years of saying I will start next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop putting off the first visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mirela to look at the date with me, not fill in the form for me. If the college cannot offer a confirmed free place outside work, I would ask about another date and keep the paid job rather than miss a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the current budget settle the 2036 choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would check the wages, bills and physical demands that exist then. A beginner taster now does not make me a qualified repairer in ten years, and I would need the right skills for whatever paid role was actually advertised.

say: I'd put **dates on preparation** rather than rely only on protection.
I'd separate **2036 thinking exposure** from 2039 hands-on robots.
think: I expect **our wages** to cover bills securely over the next few years.
My habit of **postponing learning** could waste a decade before I turn 37.
do: Save **75 monthly** only while actual wages cover rent, food, bills and travel.
Attend **free supervised taster** outside paid shifts only with confirmed place; otherwise keep paid job and seek another date.
Apply after **2036 displacement** only to actual repair vacancies whose written pay plus my partner's real wage covers the household budget.
feel: **Uneasy** about later change, secure about near-term household income.
S4.quote: A date in my diary is more useful than ten years of saying I will start next month.
fieldNote: His **near-term security** supports uneasy while the 2036 career problem remains real.
The **taster** tests an unfamiliar skill without paying fees or giving up wages.

steps.text: Save 75 monthly only while actual wages cover rent, food, bills and travel
Attend free supervised taster only with confirmed place outside paid shifts; otherwise seek another date
Seek repair roles after 2036 loss only if written pay plus partner's actual wage covers bills/travel
Keep paid insurance job if college place is unconfirmed or would cost a shift

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect my post to disappear and I would be awake over the budget. Paid notice, genuinely funded training and an actual paid opening would help; a union demand by itself is not money received.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what it feels like to be called difficult when I want to read the document myself. I can be slow to change and still care about getting the claim right. Please do not mistake my union card for a plan that has already paid the rent.

headlineQuote: Please do not mistake my union card for a plan that has already paid the rent.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old travel-claims lead** with a bachelor's degree and typical pay.
He rents with **his partner Mirela**, a pharmacy technician, and they have no children.
He has **four months saved**, some local alternatives and never uses AI tools.
He seeks **joint union terms** while testing funded practical learning cautiously.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected post loss and sleepless household calculations.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid notice**, funded training and a real paid opening would help, rather than an unagreed demand.
